title: Child Survival Strategies I: Oral Rehydration Therapy, Exclusive Breastfeeding and National Programme on Immunization
introduction: Oral Rehydration Therapy (ORT), Exclusive Breastfeeding (EBF), and the National Programme on Immunization (NPI) form three pillars of global and Nigerian child survival strategies. Together they prevent and reverse the leading causes of infant and under-five mortality—dehydration from diarrhoea, early malnutrition, and vaccine-preventable infectious diseases.
learningOutcomes: 4.1 Define Oral Rehydration Therapy (ORT), outline fluid therapy principles across dehydration severities, and compare WHO/UNICEF reduced-osmolality ORS with homemade salt-sugar-water solutions and contraindications.
4.2 Define Exclusive Breastfeeding (EBF), describe breast milk composition and hormonal lactation physiology (prolactin and oxytocin), and demonstrate proper positioning and attachment.

4.3 Manage common lactation challenges (perceived insufficient milk, engorgement, blocked duct, mastitis, sore nipples), advise on maternal diet, and explain WHO breastfeeding guidelines for HIV-infected mothers.
4.4 Define immunization, explain cold chain vaccine care, and detail the WHO/Nigeria NPI immunization schedule (contacts, target ages, vaccines, dosages, routes, and sites).
4.5 Distinguish major childhood vaccine types (BCG, diphtheria, pertussis, tetanus, measles) and identify the three true contraindications to immunization.

content.heading: Oral Rehydration Therapy (ORT): Principles, Composition, Administration, and Contraindications
content.body: Building on O'Shaughnessy's 1831 fluid-loss observations in cholera, Oral Rehydration Therapy (ORT)—defined as increased oral fluid administration paired with continued feeding—has dramatically reduced global diarrhoea deaths since 1980. Fluid therapy integrates three elements (rehydration, replacing ongoing losses, and maintenance) tailored to dehydration severity: (1) No dehydration (normal urine output)—continue normal diet/breastfeeding at home with thirst-guided fluids and maintenance solution (Na 45–60 mmol/L); (2) Mild dehydration (decreased urine output, increased thirst)—ORS 10 mL/kg/hr, reassess every 4 hours, continue breastfeeding, refeed early, and give 5–10 mL/kg extra ORS per loose stool; (3) Moderate dehydration (≥2 of sunken eyes, decreased skin turgor, dry buccal mucosa)—ORS 15–20 mL/kg/hr under observation with 4-hourly reassessment; and (4) Severe dehydration/shock (plus rapid breathing, lethargy/coma, rapid thready pulse, or skin tenting >2 seconds)—prompt IV infusion (10–20 mL/kg saline/plasma/colloid over 30 minutes) or intraosseous infusion if IV access fails. Optimal intestinal fluid uptake depends on sodium (40–90 mmol/L; >90 risks hypernatremia), glucose (110–140 mmol/L; CHO:Na ratio ≤2:1), and osmolarity (~290 mOsm/L). The official WHO/UNICEF reduced-osmolality ORS formula (total osmolality 245 mmol/L) dissolves per litre of boiled/treated water: 2.6 g NaCl (Na 75, Cl 65 mmol/L), 13.5 g anhydrous glucose (75 mmol/L), 1.5 g KCl (K 20 mmol/L), and 2.9 g trisodium citrate dihydrate (10 mmol/L). When packets are unavailable, homemade ORS uses 1 litre clean water + 2.5 mL (1/2 level tsp) salt + 30 mL (6 level tsp) sugar (discard after 12 hours at room temperature or 24 hours refrigerated; rehydration takes precedence even if only boiled/chlorinated or alternative fluids like rice water/coconut water exist). Start ORT at the first sign of diarrhoea: droppers/syringes for babies, 1 teaspoon every 1–2 minutes for under-2s (1/4–1/2 cup per loose stool; 1/2–1 cup for older children); never keep a child on ORS alone >24 hours (resume feeding within 6 hours and full diet in 24–48 hours). Short-term vomiting is NOT a contraindication (pause 5–10 minutes and resume slowly); true contraindications are protracted vomiting despite small frequent sips, worsening diarrhoea exceeding intake, stupor/coma, intestinal ileus, and hemodynamic shock with impaired airway reflexes.

content.heading: Exclusive Breastfeeding (EBF): Physiology, Composition, Positioning, and Attachment
content.body: Exclusive Breastfeeding (EBF) means an infant receives only breast milk for the first six months of life—no water, teas, herbal preparations, or solids—with the sole exceptions of ORS or prescribed drops/syrups of vitamins, minerals, or medicines. WHO recommends initiating breastfeeding within 1 hour of birth and introducing complementary solids around 6 months (when gastrointestinal, renal, and neurophysiologic maturity allow). Advantages include mother-infant bonding, lower cost than formula, ideal digestible nutrition, anti-infective protection (WBCs, antibodies, bifidus factor protecting against diarrhoea, pneumonia, diabetes, obesity, and allergies), cognitive benefits, and natural postpartum ovulation delay. Human breast milk (~4.2 g/100 mL fat [14% PUFAs], 1.1 g/100 mL protein [casein, alpha-lactalbumin, lactoferrin, IgA, IgG, lysozyme], 7 g/100 mL lactose, 0.5 g/100 mL oligosaccharides, minerals Ca/P/Na/K/Cl, and vitamins A, D, E, K, B, C) evolves from yellowish, protein- and IgA-rich Colostrum (first days; coats GI tract for passive immunity and exerts a mild laxative effect expelling meconium and curbing bilirubin/jaundice) into thinner sweet transitional milk (days 3–4) and creamier mature milk. Lactation is governed by Prolactin (milk synthesis) and Oxytocin (milk ejection from alveoli through milk ducts into sub-areolar sinuses upon suckling); supply responds to demand, so nursing on demand increases output. Proper technique begins with antenatal education: the mother sits upright and relaxed with a flat lap, holding the baby turned toward her with head and body in a straight line, mouth opposite the nipple, and neck slightly extended. Offer the whole breast without pinching the nipple/areola or pushing it into the mouth; effective feeding produces slow, deep sucks, easy swallowing, and zero maternal pain.

content.heading: Lactation Challenges, Maternal Diet, and WHO HIV Breastfeeding Guidelines
content.body: Common obstacles shortening EBF duration include: (1) Perceived insufficient milk supply—rare in well-nourished mothers; frequent 2–3 hourly feeding reflects rapid breast milk digestion, managed by improving maternal diet, increasing feeding frequency, and avoiding formula 'top-ups' while ruling out infant illness; (2) Engorgement—hard, lumpy breasts from infrequent feeding, prevented by unrestricted early feeding and treated with milk expression and warm moist compresses; (3) Blocked duct—localized tender swelling managed by frequent feeding and gentle massage toward the nipple; (4) Mastitis—infected engorgement risking abscess if untreated, managed with milk expression and antibiotics (mastitis is NOT a contraindication to breastfeeding); (5) Sore/cracked nipples—caused by poor latch onto nipple alone, managed by correcting position, air-drying, and applying hind milk; and (6) Societal barriers (short maternity leave, employment), poor knowledge, and inadequate family/professional support. Breastfeeding mothers must avoid high-mercury fish, restrict alcohol (which transfers to milk and impairs infant motor development), and limit caffeine to ≤300 mg/day. Under WHO guidelines for HIV-infected mothers, replacement feeding is recommended only when Acceptable, Feasible, Affordable, and Safe (AFAS); otherwise, exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months (followed by gradual complementary foods alongside continued breastfeeding—and continued breastfeeding beyond 6 months for HIV-infected infants) is advised, with antiretroviral (ARV) interventions to mother or exposed infant significantly reducing postnatal HIV transmission.

content.heading: National Programme on Immunization (NPI), Vaccine Care, and Schedule
content.body: Immunization introduces a vaccine into the body to stimulate active immunity against disease and is the single most cost-effective child survival intervention in developing countries, tackling vaccine-preventable diseases responsible for ~22% of child deaths in Nigeria (originally targeting the six killer diseases by age one: Tuberculosis, Diphtheria, Measles, Poliomyelitis, Tetanus, and Pertussis). Immunization saves lives, lowers infant mortality, protects community herd immunity and future generations, promotes maternal health contacts, and saves family costs. Preserving vaccine potency depends on the Cold Chain—an unbroken refrigeration and transport network from manufacturer to injection site—protecting basic vaccines from heat degradation and direct sunlight (standard storage keeps vaccines cold, ~0–8°C [noted as 0–9°C in manual text], using heat-sensitive colorimetric indicator disks/VVM to detect spoiled vials). Nigeria's five-contact WHO/NPI schedule administers: (1) 1st Contact (At Birth)—BCG 0.05 mL Intradermal (Right upper arm) + OPV0 2 drops Oral (Mouth); (2) 2nd Contact (6 weeks)—Pentavalent 1 (DPT, HBV, Hib) 0.5 mL Intramuscular (Anterolateral thigh) + OPV1 2 drops Oral; (3) 3rd Contact (10 weeks)—Pentavalent 2 0.5 mL IM (Anterolateral thigh) + OPV2 2 drops Oral; (4) 4th Contact (14 weeks)—Pentavalent 3 0.5 mL IM (Anterolateral thigh) + OPV3 2 drops Oral; and (5) 5th Contact (9 months)—Measles 0.5 mL Subcutaneous (Left upper arm) + Yellow Fever 0.5 mL Subcutaneous (Left upper arm).

content.heading: Vaccine Types and True Contraindications to Immunization
content.body: Vaccines include WHO core antigens (diphtheria, pertussis, measles, polio, TB, yellow fever, hepatitis B in endemic zones), routine additions (rubella, mumps, varicella-zoster, Haemophilus influenzae type b), and traveller vaccines (yellow fever, cholera). Key individual vaccines: BCG (live attenuated Mycobacterium bovis protecting against disseminated miliary TB and TB meningitis), Diphtheria toxoid (formalin-inactivated exotoxin neutralizing Corynebacterium diphtheriae toxin), Pertussis vaccine (inactivated Bordetella pertussis offering substantial though incomplete protection), Tetanus toxoid (formalin-inactivated Clostridium tetani tetanospasmin producing antitoxin antibodies), and Measles vaccine (live attenuated measles virus inducing high antibody protection). Mild fever or local pain after a prior injection is NOT a reason to halt routine immunization. The three true contraindications are: (1) Severe allergic reactions to a vaccine or its components (urticaria, shock, airway obstruction); (2) Severe immunosuppression (e.g., high-dose steroids or chemotherapy—avoid live vaccines like BCG, measles, and OPV and delay 3 months post-therapy; BCG is contraindicated in symptomatic AIDS); and (3) Previous severe reactions—specifically for repeat pertussis doses: febrile/afebrile seizure within 3 days, persistent/high-pitched crying within 2 days, collapse/shock within 2 days, unexplained fever >40.5°C, or anaphylaxis.

inTextQuestions.question: What are the exact ingredient weights per litre of water in the WHO/UNICEF reduced-osmolality ORS formula?
inTextQuestions.answer: 2.6 g sodium chloride, 13.5 g anhydrous glucose, 1.5 g potassium chloride, and 2.9 g trisodium citrate dihydrate per litre (total osmolality 245 mmol/L).

inTextQuestions.question: Which two hormones govern breast milk production and ejection after childbirth, and what is the clinical value of colostrum?
inTextQuestions.answer: Prolactin (milk production) and oxytocin (milk ejection). Colostrum is rich in protein and IgA antibodies that coat the newborn's gut for passive immunity and acts as a mild laxative to expel meconium and reduce bilirubin/jaundice.

inTextQuestions.question: Is mastitis a contraindication to breastfeeding, and how should it be managed?
inTextQuestions.answer: No, mastitis is not a contraindication to breastfeeding; breast milk should continue to be expressed/fed and prescribed antibiotics administered to prevent abscess formation.

inTextQuestions.question: At what age, dose, route, and site are Measles and Yellow Fever vaccines administered in Nigeria's WHO/NPI schedule?
inTextQuestions.answer: At 9 months of age (5th contact), 0.5 mL each administered subcutaneously into the left upper arm.

saqs.question: Describe the assessment and fluid management principles for mild, moderate, and severe dehydration, and list four true contraindications to ORT.
saqs.answer: Mild (decreased urine, thirst): ORS 10 mL/kg/hr, 4-hourly reassessment, plus 5–10 mL/kg per stool. Moderate (≥2 of sunken eyes, poor skin turgor, dry mucosa): ORS 15–20 mL/kg/hr under direct observation with 4-hourly reassessment. Severe (plus rapid breathing, lethargy/coma, thready pulse, skin tenting >2 sec): rapid IV (or intraosseous) saline/plasma/colloid 10–20 mL/kg over 30 min. Contraindications to ORT: protracted vomiting despite small frequent sips, worsening diarrhoea exceeding intake, stupor/coma, intestinal ileus (and hemodynamic shock with impaired airway reflexes).

saqs.question: State the homemade WHO salt-sugar-water ORS recipe, its safe storage duration, and the administration rules for infants under 2 years and vomiting children.
saqs.answer: Homemade ORS mixes 1 litre clean/boiled water with 2.5 mL (1/2 level teaspoon) salt and 30 mL (6 level teaspoons) sugar; discard after 12 hours at room temperature or 24 hours refrigerated. Under-2 infants receive 1 teaspoon every 1–2 minutes (1/4–1/2 cup after each loose stool; babies via dropper/syringe). If vomiting occurs, pause 5–10 minutes then resume slowly.

saqs.question: Define Exclusive Breastfeeding, explain proper positioning and attachment, and counsel an HIV-positive mother on diet and WHO infant feeding guidelines.
saqs.answer: EBF gives only breast milk for the first 6 months (no water/solids except ORS, vitamins, minerals, or medicines). Proper latch: mother upright/relaxed, baby's head and body aligned facing mother, mouth opposite nipple, offering whole breast without pinching areola, slow deep sucks without pain. Diet: avoid high-mercury fish, avoid alcohol (impairs infant motor development), limit caffeine to ≤300 mg/day. WHO HIV guideline: use replacement feeding only if acceptable, feasible, affordable, and safe; otherwise exclusively breastfeed for 6 months (introducing solids thereafter while continuing breastfeeding) with maternal/infant ARVs to cut transmission.

saqs.question: Outline the complete five-contact WHO/NPI immunization schedule in Nigeria including vaccine, dosage, route, and anatomical site.
saqs.answer: 1st (Birth): BCG 0.05 mL ID (right upper arm) + OPV0 2 drops oral. 2nd (6 wks): Pentavalent 1 (DPT, HBV, Hib) 0.5 mL IM (anterolateral thigh) + OPV1 2 drops oral. 3rd (10 wks): Pentavalent 2 0.5 mL IM (anterolateral thigh) + OPV2 2 drops oral. 4th (14 wks): Pentavalent 3 0.5 mL IM (anterolateral thigh) + OPV3 2 drops oral. 5th (9 mos): Measles 0.5 mL SC (left upper arm) + Yellow Fever 0.5 mL SC (left upper arm).

saqs.question: Explain the cold chain in vaccine care and state the three true contraindications to immunization with specific pertussis-related severe reactions.
saqs.answer: The cold chain is an unbroken network of refrigeration and transport from vaccine manufacture to injection protecting vaccines from heat (>8–9°C) and direct sunlight, monitored with colorimetric heat-indicator disks. True contraindications: (1) severe allergic reaction (urticaria, shock, airway obstruction), (2) severe immunosuppression (avoid live BCG/measles/OPV; delay 3 months post-therapy; no BCG in symptomatic AIDS), and (3) previous severe reactions (for pertussis: seizure within 3 days, persistent/high-pitched crying or collapse/shock within 2 days, fever >40.5°C, or anaphylaxis).
